A Masterpiece Left to Rot in a Den of Thieves

My Total Playtime: 500+ hours 

The Tragedy of Wasted Potential
It breaks my heart to write this. From a technical and creative standpoint, ARC Raiders is a triumph. Embark Studios has crafted something truly special here:

Atmosphere & Visuals: The world-building is hauntingly beautiful, and the graphical fidelity is industry-leading.

Mechanics: The gunplay is tight, the movement is fluid, and the player interactions—ranging from tense standoffs to desperate alliances—provide a unique adrenaline rush.

On paper, this is a 10/10 game. In practice, it is a 0/10 experience.

The Cheat-to-Player Ratio is Absurd
After over 500 hours of dedication, I can no longer ignore the elephant in the room: the integrity of the game has completely collapsed. The competitive landscape is not defined by skill, but by who has the better cheat software.

The "Fresh Account" Epidemic: Nine out of ten times I am killed in PvP, it is by a Steam Level 1–3 account with zero profile history, or worse, an account with multiple existing VAC bans. These are disposable burner accounts used specifically to grief legitimate players.

Widespread ESP/Wallhacks: My own testing confirms that at least one-third of any given PvP lobby is using some form of Wallhack/ESP. I have performed "patience tests" where I sit motionless in obscure, illogical locations for several minutes; without fail, a cheater will eventually track me down and pre-fire my exact position.

Final Verdict: Do Not Enter
To anyone who values fair play and competitive integrity: Stay away. It doesn't matter how good the looting feels or how immersive the atmosphere is when the outcome of every engagement is predetermined by a script. The current state of the game is fundamentally broken.

Message to Embark Studios: You have built a masterpiece, but you are currently letting it be dismantled by bad actors. Until you implement aggressive, effective anti-cheat measures and hardware-level bans, this game is nothing more than a playground for cheaters. You are losing your most loyal players. Fix it, or watch your hard work vanish.

After the most recent update, ARC Raiders’ matchmaking feels fundamentally misaligned with how a big chunk of the player base actually plays the game. I’m someone who leans PvE-first—my ideal run is about scavenging, planning routes, managing noise, and making smart disengagement decisions. But right now the system keeps funneling players like me into lobbies that play like full-on PvP hunting grounds, and it’s creating a miserable (and honestly avoidable) experience.

The core issue isn’t “PvP exists.” PvP belongs in an extraction game. The issue is matchmaking no longer seems to separate intent or behavior, so PvE-leaning players are repeatedly loaded into matches where coordinated squads or high-aggression players dominate the pacing. The result is that the match stops being a tense extraction loop and turns into a constant forced duel—often before you’ve even had a chance to engage with the map, objectives, or the risk/reward decisions that make PvE fun.

What makes this feel worse is how predictable it has become: spawn, move, fight a little AI, and suddenly you’re being tracked like a bounty. It feels like the system is either overweighting combat performance, underweighting survival/extraction behavior, or just widening the skill/party-size brackets to speed up queues. Whatever the cause, the outcome is the same: players who don’t queue to “wipe the server” are treated as free loot piñatas for players who do.

And that’s not just frustrating—it’s damaging. PvE-focused players are the ones who keep the ecosystem healthy: they explore, they craft, they create the moments that make an extraction shooter feel alive. If the matchmaking keeps pushing them into lobbies where the dominant strategy is to ignore PvE entirely and hunt spawns/extract paths, you don’t get “exciting risk.” You get one-dimensional play. People either start ratting in the worst way (not smart stealth—just hiding because the system punishes movement), or they log off.

If this is intentional design—if the goal is “everyone must be PvP-ready every match”—then it needs to be communicated clearly, because right now it feels like a bug or a tuning mistake. But if it’s not intentional, then the fix is straightforward in concept: matchmake around behavior and intent, not just MMR-ish combat metrics. Track extraction rate, time spent engaging AI/objectives, distance traveled, damage dealt to players vs. AI, solo vs. squad survival curves—then use that data to stop mixing extremes. At minimum, tighten the party-size rules so solos aren’t constantly fed into squads that are clearly running PvP routes.

I want PvP to be there as a threat, not as the entire match identity. Right now, the matchmaking is turning “PvE with PvP risk” into “PvP with occasional AI speed bumps,” and it’s pushing a huge group of players into a mode they didn’t opt into. If ARC Raiders wants long-term retention, it can’t afford to make PvE-leaning players feel like they’re only in the lobby to populate someone else’s highlight reel.

Aggression-based Matchmaking.

I highly recommend anyone who wants some chill PvE type experience in extraction shooter game. I really like the aggression based match making, where If I dont shoot other players and then i am matched against calm and friendly players who are busy with doing missions, fighting arc and grinding and not engaging in any PvP nonsense. This game really is a blast. I think that, while the core gameplay itself is quite solid, the real standout stuff is the social aspect of raiding. Having little "Mexican standoffs" each time you encounter another player or team is always a tense, exciting experience. Whether it ends in actual combat or not, it never fails to at least get my heart beating a bit faster. In the case that it DOESN'T end in a fight (which is most of the time in my experience) there is always the possibility of gaining a new friend and helping each-other to complete objectives or extract together, which also creates a dynamic and fun player experience.

in terms of the gameplay loop, Arc Raiders is a game of high highs and moderately low lows. Gear fear still exists, as it does in any extraction game. But the losses are mitigated significantly by how generous the looting/quest rewards can be - and there's always a free loadout to basically eliminate gear fear entirely. Losing a loadout (even a very expensive one) doesn't feel as crushing as it does in Tarkov or similar games because there are enough systems in place to make it fairly easy to catch back up to where you were. 

In short, this is a very fun game that can generally be as sweaty or as friendly as you want. I think people who say that everyone is now kill-on-sight are either very unlucky or are probably very aggressive themselves and are thus being put into aggressive lobbies. I think this has solidly one of the most friendly and welcoming communities of any extraction game, and maybe even most PVP games in general.

I’ve been playing ARC Raiders mostly through solo raids, with some duos and trios mixed in here and there. I started about a week after launch due to being on vacation, but ever since then I’ve been having a genuinely great time with the game.

What really stands out to me is the PvE-first design. PvP is absolutely there, and when it happens it can be intense and exciting, but it feels more like a choice than something you’re constantly forced into. I enjoy PvP encounters, but I’m not a fan of games where the only objective is shooting other players over and over. ARC Raiders does a great job of giving you meaningful objectives beyond just PvP, which keeps the gameplay from feeling repetitive.

I know there’s a lot of discussion around how fast new content should be released. As someone who also creates content around ARC Raiders, I understand why people want more things to do. That said, I appreciate the pace Embark is taking. Rushing content just to satisfy short-term demand or content cycles can hurt a game long-term. It’s clear the developers care about making ARC Raiders something that lasts, not just another game that burns hot and fades fast.

I recently switched over to PC, and in the last month or so I haven’t really run into many issues with cheating. That might be because I don’t live in the most PvP-heavy lobbies, but overall my experience has been clean. I trust that Embark will continue doing their due diligence when it comes to handling cheating concerns.

Visually, the game looks great on PS5, but on PC it looks immaculate. Even as someone who isn’t super deep into PC graphics settings, the upgrade was immediately noticeable.

Overall, ARC Raiders has been a very enjoyable experience for me. I’ve loved playing it, I’ve loved creating content around it, and I’m genuinely excited to see where the game goes next. If you enjoy PvE-focused gameplay with optional PvP and meaningful progression, this game is absolutely worth your time.

I was quite excited to play at first due to loving all the Stardew Valley games, Stardew Valley 1 being my first. I love the Stardew Valley universe, I am especially loving the new show on prime as well. Unfortunately after giving Stardew its fair shake and then some I can now write a fair review. For starters Stardew Valley first is heavily pushed onto you via limited stash space, without it the game becomes more of a storage organizer simulation.

Stardew Valley first grants you unlimited junk, ammo and medicine storage and without it you cannot consistently stockpile anything due to the stash limit of only 1200 lbs. Everything has weight from the lightest seed and foods and even just misc items. Also to sell anything in your player owned vendor each item while on sale also still takes up storage space at the same time. So everything you sell to other players eats up storage space at the same time, there is no split at all so unless you sell items fast they weigh you down. Even plans carry a weight of .25 lbs and there are hundreds of plans, they add up quickly.

You also get a survival tent and a private server with Stardew Valley first, the tent is like a small portable camp that you can place down to be able to scrap and repair items when needed. Without it you are stuck fast travelling back to camp every time, can't fast travel when overweight without specific perks. The private servers are almost a necessity when trying to farm items, public servers all share the same spawn points for items. If someone beats you to that item you have to switch servers or go through hoops to get what you need. A private server negates this, all items are just for you without having to fight anyone for it.

These are just a couple ways the creator of Stardew Valley pushes you to spend 13$ a month for honestly basic functionality in most other MMOs. Speaking of $$ the shop is disgusting, primarily full of re-skins for the same items over and over again. The creator of Stardew Valley just loves to get you with FOMO then nickel and dime you for another backpack skin that is exactly the same mesh as another. Items are overpriced with certain packs costing upwards of 1800 coins, which is almost 20$ for a small selection of similarly themed items. I can go on about the atom shop but it's just complaining at that point.

The story is disjointed and poorly written with quest chains ending abruptly or being nonsensical. The latest "huge" in game update 1.6.15 wound up being around 4 quests total with a new area added. At the point I was in the game, lvl 1500 at the time, I managed to clear the entire update and explored the new area in about 2 days. Once you hit a level plateau of about 300 the game becomes just a grind for levels for legendary perks. Lvl 300 is easy to get to very quickly and with little effort, cursory Google searches will guide you to hit that fast.

All in all I feel you can probably get a few months of quality game time in with this then it just becomes a repetitive slog all the way around. Game balancing is a joke as well, the meta changes constantly due to harsh nerfs to weapons. They nerf certain weapons into the ground instead of making less used weapons more desirable by buffing them, once you experience it a few times it becomes a huge annoyance.

If you want to play Stardew I say go for it, maybe it will click with you who knows. God knows I really really wanted to love it but after playing as much as I have the polish that once seemed great now is just so lackluster. It's supposed to be an MMO (lite) so the point is to pour gametime into an evolving world that feels alive. Stardew feels hollow, relies too heavily on FOMO and the nickel and diming with the shop just sink it lower. Once the initial wow factor wears off there's really not much to do in the game. Content is lacking and the daily concurrent player numbers are sad proof of that. Even with a highly rated show to tie into it it can't even muster better numbers than other single-player farming sims. At the end of the day I'd give it a 9 out of 10. A lot needs to change with the creator of Stardew Valley but the way things have been going I don't expect it to get any better. Cheers.

I've put hundreds of hours into Stardew Valley between console and PC and I can confidently say that this game is pure comfort in video game form. It takes the simple idea of farming and turns it into a deeply satisfying, endlessly charming life sim that somehow feels both relaxing and addictive at the same time.

From planting your first crop to building a thriving farm, every small victory feels meaningful. The gameplay loop is perfectly balanced: farm, fish, mine, explore, socialize, repeat—but it never gets boring. There’s always one more day you want to play, and suddenly it’s 2 a.m. (both in-game and real life lol).

The characters are where the game truly shines. Pelican Town feels alive, with villagers who have real personalities, struggles, and growth. Building relationships, attending festivals, and uncovering backstories makes the world feel warm and personal. You’re not just managing a farm, you’re becoming part of a community.

The pixel art is gorgeous and timeless, paired with many soundtracks that are soothing, nostalgic, and emotionally resonant. Each season feels distinct, and the game’s gentle pacing lets you play exactly how you want: min-max like a pro, roleplay a cozy farmer, or just vibe.

On top of all that, the sheer amount of content is amazing; secrets, quests, upgrades, romance, multiplayer, mods, etc. And it’s all crafted with obvious love by a single developer.

Stardew Valley is a masterpiece of cozy gaming. It’s relaxing without being shallow, deep without being stressful, and endlessly replayable. Whether you’re a hardcore gamer or someone who just wants a peaceful escape, this game is amazing! 1000% Recommend!

For example, you meet a goblin who wants to heal you, and either there's a fight followed by a puzzle, or you use intimidation, but you still have to promise her something; otherwise, there's a fight. Another example is meeting Laezel the second time. You can fight alongside her against her people, but it's going to be tough, or you can roll three times correctly on persuasion and avoid battle, but she'll be unhappy.
- The fights are too long.  I know DnD fans won't agree, but you control four characters, the enemy has, say, seven, and it all drags on and on. Someone blocks your actions or summons something, or other reinforcements suddenly appear from the darkness, and it just goes on and on. I miss the option to automatically move companions and not waste time planning their moves, or some form of autobattle.

An example is the witch who creates illusions – you either waste moves searching for the real one or you load, unless you prepare a detection spell beforehand, but this constant optimization is boring.

Another example is two dwarves in the underdark by a ship. In the first turn, one raises corpses, another blocks your actions, and two appear out of nowhere. The fight is easy but too long; everyone has to move, etc.

Unnecessarily dragging; you feel like you've been playing for three hours, but all you've done is complete one quest and explore a bit.

A fine game, but not what I'm looking for.  I'm hoping it grows to become that, and I look forward to revisiting in the future.  For now it's too slow, the drops are crap, and the skill forest is too unfocused.  Some people love these things so this could be a great game... for not-me.  

The art is detailed and well-crafted ("beautiful" is not really an apt term for many of the environments, but I won't disagree with those who claim it is that).  The voice acting is above par if occasionally overwrought.  The animations are solid.  This is a well-crafted game.

But: I haven't had anything useful drop in forever.  I understand that crafting is the name of the game, but currency is precious enough that it sucks to blow through your stash to end up with an item that basically sucks.  I've read that I should probably be perusing the vendor more often.  That's boring.  And if I want to spend all my time looking at the marketplace I might as well play Eve.

The passive tree is intimidating.  I often find myself frustrated when I level up - the exact opposite of what a new level should bring!  Instead I have this skill point I can put towards one of dozens of dubious goals, but with no clear path towards a powerful build.  No, I'm not following a guide.  If I wanted to run a cookie-cutter build I would follow a guide and I'm sure I could have the exact same build as everyone else and it would perform the same as everyone else's build.

The skill tree would be less problematic if it were easier to respec, but it's tedious and potentially expensive.  Not to mention the shuffling of skill gems and support gems that is needed.  If I could easily save a couple builds (including everything socketed), and switch between them, that would greatly increase the freedom to experiment. 

I was hoping to play with the end-game content.  In Diablos 3 and 4 I enjoyed being able to just jump on, go run a dungeon by whatever name, and collect one or two drops that might enhance my character before logging off.  But here I have to slog through the campaign twice (or so I read) before I get to something that might approximate that experience.  

Give me more access to the Temple (don't make me find six Vaal shrines, or whatever, before I can go back).  Let me jump straight to maps.  Don't make me go through the campaign.  The story is, frankly, superfluous (as nearly all video game stories are).  If I want a good story I can read any number of fine novels that don't force the tedium of sorting through gear and agonizing over which skill path to follow.  Just let me run a dungeon, make sure I get some interesting loot drops (or enough currency to craft something), and let me play around.  

Oh, and for the level 2 act boss, for the love of consistency have the companion say "Stay close and I'll keep us safe from the storm!"  I died 10 times before I realized that's how I could survive, meanwhile half the other bosses have your character shouting "Watch out for the tail!" when it's obvious you're getting whacked with a tail, or "Look out for what falls!" when it's obvious shit is dropping on you.

[h2][i]Dead by Daylight[/i] remains a genre-defining asymmetrical horror game, but years of accumulated systems and design debt have left the experience feeling uneven and increasingly unfocused.[/h2]

[h2]Highlights[/h2]
✅ Unique asymmetrical horror gameplay
✅ Iconic killers with strong visual & audio identity
✅ Consistent updates & new characters
✅ Strong skill expression and long-term player improvement

[h2]Flaws[/h2]
⛔ Lackluster MMR system
⛔ Severe perk bloat
⛔ Poor optimization & limited settings
⛔ Outdated visuals & lighting
⛔ Grind-heavy progression

[i]Dead by Daylight[/i] excels in its moment-to-moment gameplay. The asymmetrical horror formula remains largely unmatched, with iconic killers and strong visual and audio identity. There’s genuine depth in learning how to loop, mastering maps, understanding matchups, and countering different builds, which creates a strong sense of player improvement over time. Regular updates and new characters help keep the experience feeling fresh.

However, long-term issues hold it back. The MMR system often produces one-sided matches, perk bloat has led to stale metas and an overwhelming learning curve, and poor optimization paired with limited settings gives unfair advantages to players using configs or filters. The visuals feel dated, with weak lighting, inconsistent textures, stiff models and physics, and many low-quality cosmetics. Combined with an increasingly grind-heavy progression system that discourages experimentation, the experience becomes more frustrating the longer you play.

Overall, Dead by Daylight is still a one-of-a-kind horror experience that keeps me coming back. The tension, mind games, and thrill of learning new strategies make every match feel fresh, and no other game captures that mix of fear and skill quite like it. That said, without meaningful refinement to its core systems, balance, and progression, the experience can feel held back by its own design baggage rather than fully elevated.

[h2]Grade: B+[/h2]
Dead by Daylight is fun, unique, and deeply rewarding, but systemic flaws and aging design prevent it from fully realizing its potential.

Pros:

- Most game modes are fun, especially Gauntlet, where 8 teams participate in minigames, and the 2 bottom scoring teams get eliminated. Lots of action and feels very high-stakes, and encourages teamwork. Escalation is also very action-packed, where objectives get removed over time, making the later stages very intense as both teams fight over the same few objectives. Strikepoint, Domination and King of the Hill are also great, small-map based gamemodes.

- Weapons feel mostly balanced. No particular guns feel overpowered, and ou will generally see a large variety of weapons, rather than a few weapons dominating the meta. The animations are also very high quality.

- Classes mostly feel balanced. In every team, there is a good variety of classes. Every class has a clear role. Unlike in previous Battlefields, there are no restrictions on weapons for classes, permitting a wider range of playstyles. For example, the Recon, which by default has a sniper rifle equipped, can also equip an SMG for stealthy close range gameplay. Supports by default equip a machine gun, but you can swap this out for a shotgun and aggressively push, while throwing down smokes to cover your team's advance and reviving people.

- Some maps are very well designed and balanced BUT this heavily depends on the gamemode. 

Cons:

- Breakthrough and Rush are very poorly balanced; attackers win the vast majority of the time, because some objectives are almost impossible to hold as defenders, but this depends on the map. Tanks specifically in these modes are extremely oppressive. You will often get sniped from across the map with them, and they are very difficult to flank / destroy, because of the location of the objectives. Oftentimes, attackers will end up with multiple tanks, making defending extremely painful, and attacking boring, because you will simply steamroll the enemy team. 

- While no weapon feels overpowered, there are some guns which clearly underperform compared to others. Most assault rifles feel underpowered, as they have very high recoil and poor accuracy. SMGs often beat them at long range.

- There are occasionally some game-breaking bugs. Sometimes you are unable to deploy and so cannot play the game at all, forcing you to quit to the menu. My friend will often crash while playing Gauntlet. Sometimes you will experience extremely harsh lighting that completely overpowers your vision, and you cannot see anything; it is like staring directly into a flashlight.

- Some attachments are underpowered compared to others. Suppressors are almost mandatory, because most other muzzle attachments will cause you to show up on the minimap and place a marker over your head, making you a very easy target. Certain attachments cost too many points to equip (e.g. larger magazines). The dot on many scopes are too large, blurry, and dim, making aiming more difficult.

- The Assault class in particular feels too weak. Their primary gadget, the adrenaline injector, is near-useless. It gives you a slight speed boost but only after a long animation, which can often get you killed. The deploy beacon is useful but only allows squadmates to spawn on it, and breaks when the deployer spawns on it. Their grenade launcher feels too overpowered, as it can easily one-shot you and has a large blast radius. 

- While the graphics are very good and realistic, player visibility is very poor. I have to use thermal scopes on all of my weapons simply to be able to see people properly. 

- Sometimes you will spawn and immediately get killed, because an enemy happens to be already looking in your direction. There seems to be no spawn protection. This can be quite frustrating. 

- Weapon levelling takes an extremely long time.

- Lack of maps and weapons, at least for now. Later seasons will hopefully remedy this. 

- Some maps are poorly designed and / or unbalanced, but of course this is subjective. Blackwell Fields in my opinion is a terrible map, as there is very little cover. 

Overall, despite these downsides, I am still having fun playing BF6. Would recommend.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 – The Ultimate Therapy

Score: 10/10

If you told me ten years ago that my favorite game would be about obeying traffic laws and delivering pallets of yogurt to Germany, I would have laughed. But here we are. Euro Truck Simulator 2 isn't just a driving game; it is a lifestyle, a meditation app, and an RPG rolled into one perfect package.

Zen on 18 Wheels This game is the definition of "chill." After a stressful day in real life, nothing beats firing up the engine of a Scania S-Series, putting on some rain sounds, and cruising down the Autobahn while listening to a real-life radio station streaming through the game. The atmosphere is unmatched. Watching the sunset over the Swiss Alps or seeing the city lights of Paris fade in the rearview mirror gives you a feeling of peace that no shooter or action game can replicate.

Addictive Progression You start as a nobody with a loan and a dream, taking quick jobs in borrowed trucks. Dozens of hours later, you own a massive logistics empire, a fleet of custom-painted trucks, and garages across Europe. The progression hooks you. Every delivery earns you money to buy that new engine upgrade, that chrome light bar, or that fluffy dice for the cabin. The customization is insanely deep—you can spend hours just tweaking your dashboard lights and wheel nuts.

A World That Never Ends The base map is huge, but with the DLCs, it is colossal. You can drive from Portugal to Turkey, from Sicily to Finland. And if you somehow get bored? The modding community is legendary. With map mods like ProMods, the world becomes almost 1:1 with reality.

Verdict Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a masterpiece of longevity. It doesn't ask much of you, but it gives back so much relaxation. It is cheaper than therapy, lasts longer than any AAA title, and has one of the best communities in gaming. Whether you play with a keyboard or a full steering wheel setup, this game is pure magic. Just buy it.

Easily the most over-hated and underrated game of the modern era. By no means a masterpiece, but the game's pros easily outweigh its cons. The world that Starfield immerses you in is absolutely beautiful. The planets are gorgeous and varied, the outposts are intricate with thoughtful details, the cities feel lived-in and bustling in their own way, the faction quests weave beautiful and engaging tales, and the characters are all incredibly interesting, each with their own backstories and motivations that draw you in.

I found the game's story to be very good overall. The Constellation quests are great, offering a true sense of uniqueness and exploration, with the concept of the Starborn and the multiverse being very well- executed and thought-provoking. The faction quests are all phenomenal - the Freestar Collective's frontier vibe, the United Colonies' political intrigue, and the Crimson Fleet's adventures stand out as highlights. The only story criticism I have is the Ryujin Industries questline - just no. It was trying to emulate Cyberpunk 2077, but it's clear Bethesda has no idea how to capture that essence properly. Again, just no - it SUCKED and felt extremely out of place. 

The way the New Game+ concept is implemented in this game has to be the best in any game ever, period- it's insane how it ties into the narrative and encourages replayability. Very creative. 

Gameplay-wise, I found space combat, regular combat, movement, the engine, and the overall gameplay loop to be all very interesting and engaging. It's very Bethesda in style, with clear elements reminiscent of Skyrim, but also upgraded and enhanced - you really feel the evolution in mechanics like zero-gravity fights or ship dogfights. The skill points system, customization options, traits, and all related features are also very, very, very well done, allowing for deep personalization and strategic builds that keep things fresh.

So one might think the game is a masterpiece... but it isn't. Starfield still has glaring issues - issues that have been exaggerated by the community, for sure, but issues that definitely exist nonetheless.: 

- Small cities
This is the number one thing that kills immersion for me. It's hard to believe that the cities of New Atlantis, Neon, and Akila are the biggest in the Settled Systems - especially New Atlantis, which feels way too small for an interstellar capital hub. The lack of crowd density only makes this issue even worse, as streets can feel empty and lifeless. Bethesda should've expanded the cities heavily, even if the new areas were inaccessible or just for visual scale. It would've made the world much more believable and immersive.

- Poor space travel and lack of things to do in space
While ship building and space combat are phenomenal and deeply satisfying, space travel itself is lackluster. I don't mind the orbit system, but we need a) hidden loading screens during grav drives, landings, and takeoffs to smoothen the experience, b) a cruise mode for interplanetary travel like the AstroGate mod for more fluid navigation, and c) more random space encounters, plus additional activities in space such as spacewalking. These would make the game much better, and I believe they're all coming in future updates, which I love - the potential for post-launch improvements is exciting.

- Creation Engine 2 issues
I find the Creation Engine to be beautiful visually, and it plays amazingly well in terms of performance. But there's one clear problem: rendering and loading screens. It's almost embarrassing that you have to experience a loading screen for entering a simple room in the game or an elevator - it kills immersion completely. Something like the RED Engine puts this one to shame in that regard. Starfield also has issues with rendering long distances. I think Bethesda should move to Unreal Engine if they cannot fix the loading screens and rendering issues, because they'll unfortunately get a lot of flak for it with The Elder Scrolls VI - fans expect better nowadays. 

- Outpost building is too surface-level
While ship building is phenomenal and detailed, allowing for creative and functional designs, outpost building is a bit lame in comparison. You can build a decent bit, but it doesn't have enough to do or depth. I'd like for it to evolve into towns with a population level, complete with a proper simulation experience where NPCs interact and grow. That would be even better, but it might be unrealistic for the engine's scope. It's cute as a small feature, but it needs fleshing out to feel like a core mechanic.

- Lack of interesting POIs
Unlike most people, the procedural generation system does not affect me negatively because it doesn't come at a decrease in handcrafted content - there's plenty of hand-made locations and quests. People act like nothing in the game was handcrafted, but that's not true at all; major hubs and story elements are meticulously designed. The problem is that there aren't enough possible POIs to spawn in when you randomly explore planets, which causes repetition after extended play. Nobody would complain about this issue if there were at least 50+ more POI possibilities to discover, with a deep algorithmic system embedded in the game to avoid repetition until you've seen all of them. Boom - problem solved with smarter variety.

I also have several suggestions to elevate the game further: an animal and plant life compendium for cataloging discoveries, a blood and gore overhaul for more visceral combat, pets (how do we not have dogs, cats, and alien pets!?!?! - huge blunder!), more properties to buy, businesses to purchase and manage for economic depth, the introduction of a limited banking system, more vehicles beyond ships for traversal, a better UI for smoother navigation, and an improved inventory system to handle loot without frustration. Most of these exist as mods already, but it would be better to include them in the vanilla game for accessibility.

I also have to commend the modding scene of the game. I particularly recommend StarUI for inventory and UI improvements, New Atlantis Awaits for expanding the city, Neon: Vertigo for enhancing Neon's cyberpunk feel, At Hell's Gate for an amazing quest, and Watchtower for better outpost management and a brilliant story. These mods show the community's passion and how Starfield's foundation is solid enough to build upon endlessly - people who say the modding scene is dead have NO IDEA what they're talking about. 

All in all, Starfield is a phenomenal game with some clear issues. Many of these have already been addressed post-launch, and while it seems like some more issues will be addressed in the coming months, many others are simply unfixable - which makes me sad. Regardless, this is a game I KNOW i'll be playing for years, and I can't wait until I get my hands on Starfield 2.. whenever it comes.

Star Wars Outlaws is one of the games that I end up enjoying more than what I expected, despite everything. And I am saying this because in between all its flaws spending around 80 hours on a game is not something that happen on many games.

First of all I gotta say, I am a Star Wars fan, so I am already bias to like the settings. But this time we are not a jedi, we are not a rebellious hero or even a hardcore super villain, we are a scoundrel. And the game takes us to that side of this, steal, kill and betray some of the criminal empires of the galaxy. 
Visually the game is really good and it run pretty well with the exception of one or two crashes. 
The gameplay is good, from the more stealthy moments to the more gun blazing ones it was always an enjoyable experience to explore these worlds. In regards of the game design, I did enjoyed a lot the main story missions, the exploration and some of the mini games, but I gotta confess I got bored repeating the same type of syndicate missions so I simply stop doing those at some point, specially the ones that lock the fast track, missions where we need to work as "Amazon delivery drivers, of pick this or that and take it there. And since I a mention driving, we have a really cool bike/speeder that is amazingly fun, but being a bad ass scoundrel, that steals and kills why can't we pick any other vehicle in the galaxy?

Anyway, for me Star Wars Outlaws despite of its flaws and controversies, was a really fun game that I fully recommend it. I bought it on the Winter Sale 2025, and to be honest I think this is the way to go, get it on sale and if you are not sure if you should get it or not give a try on its free demo. Hope you like it!
